analysis.one_liner: Slaps a 30% tax and a U.S. entry ban on people who renounce citizenship to dodge taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: introduced in May 2012, it sat in the Senate Finance Committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set a 30% tax on capital gains earned in the U.S. by people who gave up their citizenship for tax reasons, and required withholding of that tax at the source. It would also have made those former citizens legally inadmissible to the United States, with only a narrow waiver if they first paid what their renunciation cost the Treasury. It was a direct response to the public furor over a billionaire Facebook co-founder renouncing U.S. citizenship ahead of the company's stock offering, though the bill itself does not name him.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who would no longer see the wealthiest people legally opt out of the U.S. tax system while continuing to enjoy U.S. markets and the right to visit; the bill targets people whose gains come from selling U.S. assets [S3]. The Treasury would collect tax that currently escapes when someone renounces citizenship and later sells U.S. assets [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 30% tax on net capital gains from U.S. sources realized by a 'specified expatriate' — someone who renounced citizenship within the last 10 years and cannot show the renunciation did not cut their taxes — and requires the tax be withheld at the source [S2] [S3].

Bars such former citizens from re-entering the United States, with no automatic waiver; Treasury, State, and Homeland Security would have a year to design a waiver policy that could require paying a tax or penalty equal to the revenue the person's expatriation cost the government [S2] [S3].

Closes a real gap in current law: under existing rules a former citizen generally pays no U.S. capital-gains tax on later sales of U.S. assets, so someone can renounce, hold U.S. stock, and sell it tax-free [S3].

analysis.who_pays: People who renounce U.S. citizenship primarily to cut their tax bills — overwhelmingly very wealthy individuals — who would face a 30% tax on U.S. capital gains, withholding, and the loss of the right to enter the country unless they settle up with the Treasury [S2] [S3]. Anyone renouncing citizenship would have the burden of proving to the Treasury Secretary that taxes were not their motive to avoid the penalty [S3].

drawbacks.text: The presumption of tax avoidance applies broadly: any covered expatriate in the 10-year window is treated as a tax dodger unless they prove to the Treasury Secretary that their renunciation did not substantially reduce their taxes, which penalizes people who renounce for personal or family reasons and are wealthy enough to be 'covered expatriates' [S3].

Denying re-entry is a heavy sanction that reaches beyond tax collection — an expatriate would be barred from visiting family or doing business in the U.S. — and the waiver would not exist on day one, only as a policy Treasury must propose to Congress within a year [S2] [S3].
The bill raises little revenue in absolute terms because renunciation is rare, so its main effect is symbolic and punitive rather than a meaningful fix to the tax code.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real, if narrow, loophole: wealthy people can renounce citizenship and later sell U.S. assets largely free of U.S. capital-gains tax [S3]. The remedy is blunt — a presumption of tax avoidance that the individual must rebut, plus a re-entry ban — and would catch some people whose reasons were not taxes, though an exception exists for those who can prove no substantial tax reduction [S3]. The revenue at stake is small because expatriation is rare, so the honest case for the bill is fairness and deterrence, not money.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Senator Schumer and three Democratic colleagues introduced the bill on May 17, 2012 [S1] [S3].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance — its only action in the chamber [S1] [S5].
The Finance Committee held no hearing, marked it up, or voted on it, and the bill never reached the Senate floor; it expired when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wealthy individuals who renounce citizenship to cut their taxes are better off: the loophole the bill would have closed remains open. The Senate Finance Committee, by not acting, preserved the status quo for them.

for.name: Sen. Charles Schumer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Ex-PATRIOT Act and recruited three Democratic cosponsors

for.name: Sens. Robert Casey, Richard Blumenthal, and Tom Harkin

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Max Baucus (D-MT)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsor signed on, and the Democratic-controlled Finance Committee declined to act on the bill before the Congress ended [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill's entire purpose is to end the ability of wealthy people to renounce citizenship and keep avoiding U.S. tax on U.S. capital gains; it would tax those gains at 30% and bar re-entry unless they settle up [S2] [S3]. Their gain is the public's cost, since the assets and gains come from U.S. markets and infrastructure.
A large advisory industry helps wealthy clients structure renunciation and offshore holdings to minimize U.S. tax; a 30% withholding regime with a re-entry ban would shrink that business [S2] [S3].
